title: Could Spider-Man Really Turn Off His Powers? Real Science Says Maybe
summary:
Slight movie spoilers ahead! In Spider-Man: Brand New Day, Peter Parker has troubling symptoms caused by spider DNA from the bite that gave him his powers. He wants to get rid of some of his spider traits but keep others. So he visits Bruce Banner, who invented a device to keep his alter ego, the Hulk, in check. It is a superpower inhibitor.

The movie device is based on real science. Small interfering RNAs, or siRNAs, are real molecules that can turn off certain genes. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration has approved at least eight siRNA treatments for genetic diseases.

Here is how they work. Genes are pieces of DNA that hold instructions for building a living thing. A cell copies those instructions into messenger RNA, or mRNA. Then other parts of the cell read the mRNA to build proteins, which do jobs in the body. An siRNA grabs onto a specific mRNA and marks it to be chopped up. That stops the protein from being made, which silences the gene.

Anastasia Khvorova, a chemical biologist at the University of Massachusetts Chan Medical School, says shutting down foreign DNA, such as spider DNA, is something siRNAs do well. If Spider-Man's powers came from one gene, one siRNA could work. But Peter wants to shut off several traits, like making web silk and super-strong senses. It is rare for one gene to control such different traits, so he would probably need a mix of siRNAs.

Judy Lieberman, an immunologist at Boston Children's Hospital, says slowing a protein down might let Spider-Man control how strong his powers are. But no one has been able to tune siRNAs that precisely yet.
why_it_matters: The movie shows how real gene-silencing medicine works, a tool already used to treat genetic diseases and still being improved.

background_read: In the comics and movies, Peter Parker gains his powers after being bitten by a special spider, which is how he becomes Spider-Man.
Every living cell carries DNA, and cells copy parts of it into messenger RNA so they can build the proteins that give a living thing its traits.
RNA interference is a natural way cells turn down certain genes, and scientists have learned to design small interfering RNAs to silence genes that cause disease.
Science fiction often borrows real research, which can be a fun way to learn how the real science works and where its limits are.
